opening: Leadership is often judged by what an individual builds, the organisations they lead and the professional milestones they achieve.
But there is another dimension to leadership that deserves equal attention: what an individual does with the opportunities and resources that success brings.
body: For Colonel Manbeer Choudhary, this responsibility has been a consistent part of his journey.
A retired Indian Army officer, hospitality entrepreneur and philanthropist, he has moved across very different professional worlds while retaining a commitment to service.
His work in healthcare, children's welfare, support for war widows and ex servicemen, and charitable initiatives reflects a belief that professional achievement should create value beyond business.
A Foundation Built on Discipline and ServiceColonel Manbeer's outlook was shaped by his upbringing in a Jatt Sikh family with ancestral roots in Gujranwala.
His family migrated during the Partition of India, and his mother, Mrs Jaswant Kaur, took up teaching to support the family.
Her perseverance and commitment to education left a lasting impression on him.
After studying at a government aided school in Karnal, he joined the National Defence Academy and served in the Indian Army for 25 years.
The experience shaped his understanding of discipline, accountability, leadership and collective responsibility.
His decision to leave the Army to attend to his ailing father marked a significant transition.
He subsequently entered hospitality, beginning with Jewels Hotel in Karnal.

What followed was an entrepreneurial journey that led to the establishment of Noormahal Palace, now Noor Mahal by Marriott International, India's first Autograph Collection hotel, along with Hazuri Bagh in Karnal and Colonel Saab, with restaurants in London's Holborn and Trafalgar Square.
His contribution to the hospitality sector also included institutional leadership.
He served as President of the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations of India during 2005 and 2006 and as Founder President of the Hotel and Restaurant Association of Haryana.
Yet, beyond these professional milestones, his engagement with social welfare has remained a defining part of his work.
Philanthropy with a Focus on Dignity and OpportunityColonel Manbeer Choudhary's philanthropic activities span healthcare, education, nourishment and the welfare of disadvantaged communities.
He has supported charitable organisations, orphanages and institutions working with children with hearing and speech impairments.
An important part of this commitment is his association with MDD Bal Bhawan, where he has taken responsibility for supporting the orphanage initiative.
As its Founder and Trustee, his involvement reflects a commitment to children's welfare and the belief that every child deserves care, dignity and an opportunity to build a better future.
His social engagement also extends to the armed forces community.
Through his association with the Army Wives Welfare Association (AWWA), he has supported war widows through financial assistance and helped create employment opportunities.
He has also provided employment opportunities to ex servicemen in the region.
These efforts address an important aspect of social welfare: helping individuals and families who have faced difficult circumstances regain stability, dignity and economic independence.
During the COVID 19 pandemic, his hospitality establishments extended accommodation, meals and medical assistance to patients and doctors.
His support for educational initiatives, including providing computers to schools, further demonstrates his interest in practical interventions that improve access to opportunity.
The Sikh Identity and the Principle of SevaColonel Manbeer's Jatt Sikh identity is central to his personal and cultural heritage.
His family's roots in Gujranwala connect him to a region deeply associated with Sikh history, including the Sukerchakia Misl and Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
The Sikh principle of seva, or selfless service, has particular relevance to his approach to philanthropy.
For him, community responsibility is not simply an expression of identity; it is reflected in active participation, charitable contributions and support for institutions working for social welfare.
His contributions to charitable and community causes have received recognition from Gurdwara Prabandhak Committees, including HGPC, and international Sikh forums on several occasions.
These recognitions acknowledge his engagement with social welfare and his contributions within the wider Sikh community.
His work reflects an understanding that community development requires sustained involvement and a willingness to support people and institutions beyond one's immediate professional responsibilities.

A Broader Measure of SuccessColonel Manbeer Choudhary's journey brings together three distinct forms of contribution: service to the nation, institution building through entrepreneurship and service to society through philanthropy.
His military career established a foundation of discipline and duty.
His hospitality ventures demonstrated the ability to adapt and build in an unfamiliar industry.
His charitable work has provided another expression of leadership, one centred on the welfare of children, vulnerable families, war widows, ex servicemen and underserved communities.
In an environment where business success is frequently measured through scale and financial performance, his journey offers a broader perspective.
The value of an institution can also be understood through the opportunities it creates and the communities it supports.
For Colonel Manbeer, the idea of service has simply evolved with time.
It began in uniform, continued through entrepreneurship and finds expression today in philanthropy and community welfare.
His enduring contribution lies not only in the institutions he has helped build, but in his belief that the responsibility to serve society must remain an integral part of leadership.

A Foundation Built on Discipline and ServiceColonel Manbeer's outlook was shaped by his upbringing in a Jatt Sikh family with ancestral roots in Gujranwala.

stories.headline: We're being subjected to cognitive warfare by adversaries, need to bolster capabilities: CDS
stories.title: We're being subjected to cognitive warfare by adversaries, need to bolster capabilities: CDS
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 27: Chief of Defence Staff Gen N S Raja Subramani on Friday said the distinction between war and peace is "blurring" today and there is a "continuous state of contestation", cautioning that warfare in cyber, electronic and cognitive domains is already occurring. Delivering an address here on the 'Future of warfare and India's preparedness to conduct multi-domain operations', he also said, without elaborating, "We are being subjected to cognitive warfare by our adversaries in an insidious way" to weaken the will and morale of the nation, and emphasised bolstering capabilities in all domains. The general officer, during an interactive session after delivering his talk at a seminar, also asserted that "we are well-geared, along our northern frontier". Asked how he saw China successfully launching on Wednesday its Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship carrying three astronauts, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the CDS said Pakistan's space capability is "improving" with China's help, and positional navigation and other domain-related capabilities available with the Chinese will be available to the Pakistanis, so that will have to be "factored into our calculus". He also spoke on the significance of air power, and said that for bolstering the Navy's prowess, there is a need for more unmanned surface vessels, unmanned underwater vessels and enablers to increase their range. "We want to be joint in design, multi-domain in orientation, have a tech-enabled capability, be Aatmanirbhar in thought and action, and finally a capable human-centric leadership," the CDS said. Gen Anil Chauhan (retd), who was the CDS during Operation Sindoor last year, moderated the session hosted by think-tank Vivekananda International Foundation in Delhi. The CDS, in his address, outlined 10 major trends which, he said, are defining the future of warfare, underlining that the first is the expanding nature of the battlefield. "Secondly, the distinction between war and peace is increasingly (getting) blurred. We are in a state of continuous contestation. "Cyber, space, electronic warfare and cognitive warfare are already occurring, and that means they will precede a conflict, they will occur during the conflict, and they will outlast the conflict. So, we cannot say that we are either in a state of peace or war; we are in a continuous state of contestation," he said. The CDS said that in coordination with the three services, efforts are underway to "modernise our electronic warfare architecture". Elaborating his point on the idea of "continuous contestation" and the blurring of the distinction between peace and war, he said, "Even today, we are being subjected to cognitive warfare by our adversaries in an insidious manner, to sow (seeds of) division in society, create internal rifts, weaken the will and morale of the nation." "Therefore, it is important that we understand cognitive warfare and information warfare, and a commander today will have to spend as much time on operations as he has to devote time to information warfare," the CDS added. It is "not a supporting function", it is a "primary function of the commander". It is one of the important building blocks as far as multi-domain operations are concerned, he said. He cited multiple conflicts in the last few years, from the Azerbaijan-Armenia conflict to the Ukraine conflict and the US-Israel-Iran conflict. "Economically, wars in one part of the world can affect everybody... When we look at the Iran-Israel war, we see that closure of Strait of Hormuz in terms of critical minerals, fertilisers, energy is affecting each and everybody in the world, and led to loss of (US President Donald) Trump in the (US) mid-term elections. So, unintended effects," he said. "The other unintended effect as far as we are concerned is the Makkah alliance," the CDS said. Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Makkah on August 7. The pact establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all three. The CDS also cited Operation Sindoor, terming its second phase an excellent example of joint, integrated, multi-domain operations, and asserted that India not only had control over the escalation matrix and escalation dominance, but it also resulted in a "decisive victory" for India. Gen Raja Subramani underlined the evolving nature of technology and the warfare, however, cautioning that technological superiority is "only transitory" and this will need constant improvement to stay prepared for future wars. He emphasised that a whole-of-nation approach is needed to fight and sustain a prolonged war. The general officer said multiple-domain operations is not about combining all the capabilities, rather it implies integrating different capabilities to "pose multiple dilemma to an adversary". He said integration of military-space architecture and the ability to communicate effectively are key to carrying out such operations and cyber defence is an integral component of it, he added. The CDS further said an integrated command and control system is a prerequisite for conducting such operations. On military preparedness, at a time when multiple conflicts are underway, he said, "We need not look at a prescribed template. We need to have our own template."

stories.title: Supreme Court raps TVK government, orders lamp to be lit at Tamil Nadu site

The court has now permitted all devotees to light lamps at the controversial location, expressing serious concern over the state's non-compliance and the initiation of contempt proceedings. Additionally, former judges have been appointed to supervise temple matters, reinforcing the importance of adhering to the rule of law.

stories.headline: Supreme Court refuses to mandate unified portal for tracing unclaimed deposits; cites regulatory reforms
stories.title: Supreme Court refuses to mandate unified portal for tracing unclaimed deposits; cites regulatory reforms
stories.summary: Sucheta Dalal’s petition highlighted the accumulation of unclaimed deposits and investments with financial institutions and the procedural difficulties faced by nominees and legal heirs in recovering them
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (November 27, 2026) observed that regulatory reforms had substantially addressed the principal concerns raised in a plea seeking to facilitate the identification and recovery of unclaimed bank deposits, mutual fund investments and securities by legal heirs of deceased persons.
The court, however, declined to mandate the creation of a unified portal for tracing and reclaiming such assets, noting that substantial sector-specific mechanisms were already in place.
A Bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath and R. Mahadevan disposed of a public interest litigation (PIL) filed in 2022 by journalist and managing editor of Moneylife magazine Sucheta Dalal.
The PIL highlighted the accumulation of unclaimed deposits and investments with financial institutions and the procedural difficulties faced by nominees and legal heirs in recovering them.
“…we find that the principal concerns which prompted the institution of the present writ petition have been substantially addressed.

The subsequent establishment of centralised search facilities, simplification of claim procedures, strengthening of nomination and transmission mechanisms, and implementation of public awareness initiatives constitute significant progress towards addressing these concerns,” the Bench said, adding that any specific grievance concerning unclaimed financial assets may be pursued before the competent authority in accordance with law.

The petition sought directions to streamline the settlement of claims by legal heirs regarding bank deposits, insurance proceeds, post-office deposits and other financial assets to avoid unnecessary litigation.

It also stressed the need for a centralised online database under the aegis of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), providing particulars of deceased account holders, including their names, addresses and the dates of their last transactions.

The Bench noted that the RBI had launched the Unclaimed Deposits, Gateway to Access Information (UDGAM) portal in August 2023, enabling individuals to trace unclaimed deposits across multiple banks through a common platform.

The search facility was subsequently extended to 30 banks, which together accounted for approximately 90% of the unclaimed deposits held in the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF) in terms of value.

The Department of Financial Services informed the court that unclaimed financial assets worth approximately ₹6,453 crore had been returned to their rightful claimants as of April 18, 2026, through a nationwide campaign titled ‘Aapki Poonji, Aapka Adhikar’, launched in October last year.
Outreach and facilitation camps had been organised across 748 districts.

stories.headline: India's textile exporters race the tariff clock
stories.title: India's textile exporters race the tariff clock
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Exporters are also worried that this time round, they won't be able to share any tariff increase burden with buyers, as profit margins have been squeezed by rising raw material prices such as cotton and synthetic yarn.

While it refuted allegations of excess capacity-noting that existing capacity is necessary for meeting domestic demand, a market growing at around 7%-the industry has also been taken by surprise by the exclusion of competitors Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
The USTR has proposed a Section 301 tariff ceiling of up to 25% on Indian goods, with a conditional reduced rate of 17% linked to a reciprocal trade agreement.
This is likely to hit India's exports of home textiles and furnishings as well as apparel.

"The shipments for the upcoming spring and summer season, which is more important for India, as it consists mostly of cotton garments, is about to begin," said Sanjay Jain, managing director at TT Textile, a manufacturer and exporter of yarn, textile and garments.
"We will try to rush our shipments to January.
However, it will be challenging as shipping time is two months."
The industry refuted the claim of excess capacity by the US.

"Contrary to perceptions of surplus supply, India's textile and home textile sectors have no idle manufacturing capacity, as existing production is geared towards meeting both export commitments and the growing domestic demand," said Vijay Agarwal, chairman of the Creative Group, a textile exporter to the US market and former chairman of The Cotton Textile Export Promotion Council (Texprocil).

"Mills and exporters operate with tightly planned production schedules, leaving little scope to absorb sudden tariff increases or cut prices without affecting margins and operational viability," he said.
Unlike last year, when Indian garment and textile exporters shared the burden of increased import duty with US buyers, this time, exporters may have to absorb a bigger hit of any duty hike.

body: The USTR has proposed a Section 301 tariff ceiling of up to 25% on Indian goods, with a conditional reduced rate of 17% linked to a reciprocal trade agreement.
This is likely to hit India's exports of home textiles and furnishings as well as apparel.

"The shipments for the upcoming spring and summer season, which is more important for India, as it consists mostly of cotton garments, is about to begin," said Sanjay Jain, managing director at TT Textile, a manufacturer and exporter of yarn, textile and garments.
"We will try to rush our shipments to January.
However, it will be challenging as shipping time is two months." The industry refuted the claim of excess capacity by the US.

"Contrary to perceptions of surplus supply, India's textile and home textile sectors have no idle manufacturing capacity, as existing production is geared towards meeting both export commitments and the growing domestic demand," said Vijay Agarwal, chairman of the Creative Group, a textile exporter to the US market and former chairman of The Cotton Textile Export Promotion Council (Texprocil).

"Mills and exporters operate with tightly planned production schedules, leaving little scope to absorb sudden tariff increases or cut prices without affecting margins and operational viability," he said.
Unlike last year, when Indian garment and textile exporters shared the burden of increased import duty with US buyers, this time, exporters may have to absorb a bigger hit of any duty hike.
